newsitem.title: HUNGARY: ING SAYS HUNGARY COULD CUT DEVALUATION RATE IN H2.
newsitem.headline: ING SAYS HUNGARY COULD CUT DEVALUATION RATE IN H2.

text.p: A probable moderate rise in the trade deficit and a projected fall in inflation are likely to enable Hungary to cut the forint devaluation rate later this year, an ING Barings analyst said on Tuesday.

"In our view, current trade data and the anticipated H2 fall in inflation to 16 percent by December (from the current 18.8 percent) will support a further reduction in the monthly devaluation rate in early H2 to 1.0 percent," Douglas Reid said in ING's quarterly country report.
The monthly devaluation rate was reduced to 1.1 percent from 1.2 percent on April 1.
Reid said a 14-month decline in Hungary's CPI would slow down in the second quarter of 1997 due to energy price hikes, higher food costs and wage increases in the first quarter.

But in the second quarter of the year, the decline in inflation will pick up, driven mainly by lower import prices following import duty cuts, restrictive wage contracts and continuously falling inflation expectation, he said.

He added that a forecast 12 percent increase in imports and 10 percent rise in exports in 1997 are likely to bring the trade deficit to around $2.8 billion, a slight increase from $2.7 billion in 1996.
Reid added that the revenues and savings of the social security could be well below the budgeted levels this year.
The government conceded that the 10,000-hospital-bed reduction announced in 1996 would lead to savings of 1.5 billion forints, rather than the originally planned 8,5 billion forints, he said.

The revenue from the sale of assets is likely to be lower than the budgeted 10 billion forints and revenues from a new minimum social security contribution could be below the planned levels as tens of thousands of individual entrepreneurs surrendered activities due to the new rules, Reid added.
ING forecasts an overall state budget deficit of 5.3 percent of the GDP for 1997, compared with a government target of 4.9 percent.

Reid also said that the central bank's (NBH) demonstrated cautious approach to interest rate reduction made the forint likely to continue to trade at the NBH resistance level (bid) throughout 1997 and track the movements of the dollar/mark cross.
